note.text:
Multiplying in base b is like multiplying in base ten, but you carry groups of b.

Example in base 4: 23₄ × 3₄
• Units: 3 × 3 = 9. Nine is two fours and 1 more: write 1, carry 2.
• Fours: 3 × 2 + 2 = 8, which is two fours and 0 more: write 0, carry 2.
• Write the last carry, 2.
So 23₄ × 3₄ = 201₄.

Check in base ten: 23₄ = 11 and 3₄ = 3, and 11 × 3 = 33. In base 4, 33 is 201₄, because 2 × 16 + 0 × 4 + 1 = 33.

Tip: learn the multiplication table of the base. In base 4, 3 × 3 = 21₄ (two fours and one).

steps: Write the last carry, {k1}. The answer is {k1}{c1 % b}{c0 % b}{sub(b)}.
Check in base ten: {x}{sub(b)} = {fromBase(x, b)}, and {fromBase(x, b)} × {y} = {product}. In base {b}, {product} is {toBase(product, b)}{sub(b)}.
checks: str(k1) + str(c1 % b) + str(c0 % b) == toBase(product, b)

cards.idea: Multiply as you do in base ten, then write the result in base b. Knowing the base's times table helps.
example: {d * e} = {idiv(d * e, b)} × {b} + {(d * e) % b}, so in base {b} it is {toBase(d * e, b)}{sub(b)}.
checks: fromBase(toBase(d * e, b), b) == d * e

cards.idea: For a two-digit number, multiply the units first. Write what is left after taking away groups of b, and carry the number of groups.
example: Units: {y} × {dig(x, 0)} = {c0} = {idiv(c0, b)} × {b} + {c0 % b}: write {c0 % b}, carry {idiv(c0, b)}.
{b}s: {y} × {dig(x, 1)} + {idiv(c0, b)} = {c1} = {idiv(c1, b)} × {b} + {c1 % b}: write {c1 % b}, carry {idiv(c1, b)}.
checks: str(idiv(c1, b)) + str(c1 % b) + str(c0 % b) == toBase(fromBase(x, b) * y, b)

check.prompt: In base {b}, you calculate {x}{sub(b)} × {e}{sub(b)}. Which digit do you write in the units column?

misconceptions.explain: {dig(x, 0)} × {e} = {u}. Take away groups of {b}, not tens: {u} = {idiv(u, b)} × {b} + {u % b}.

solution: Write {u % b} in the units column and carry {idiv(u, b)}.

cards.idea: Check a product by changing the numbers to base ten, multiplying, and changing back.
example: {fromBase(x, b) * y} in base {b} is {toBase(fromBase(x, b) * y, b)}{sub(b)}: it matches.

check.prompt: To check a product, you first change {s}{sub(b)} to base ten. What is it?

questions.verify: fromBase(toBase(d * e, b), b) == d * e

misconceptions.explain: {d} × {e} = {d * e} in base ten. In base {b}, {d * e} is {toBase(d * e, b)}{sub(b)}.
{d} × {e} = {d * e}. Count the groups of {b} in {d * e}: {plural(idiv(d * e, b), 'group', 'groups')} and {(d * e) % b} more.
That is {d} + {e}. The question asks for {d} × {e}.

solution: {d * e} = {idiv(d * e, b)} × {b} + {(d * e) % b}, so in base {b} it is {toBase(d * e, b)}{sub(b)}.

questions.prompt: In base {b}, calculate {x}{sub(b)} × {e}{sub(b)}. Give your answer in base {b}.

misconceptions.explain: You carried in tens. In base {b}, carry one for every group of {b}.

solution: Check in base ten: {fromBase(x, b)} × {e} = {fromBase(x, b) * e}.

questions.prompt: In base {b}, calculate {x}{sub(b)} × {y}{sub(b)}. Give your answer in base {b}. (Hint: you may go through base ten.)
questions.verify: fromBase(answer, b) == fromBase(x, b) * fromBase(y, b)

misconceptions.explain: That is the base-ten product of the digits. In base {b}: {x}{sub(b)} = {n1}, {y}{sub(b)} = {n2}, and {n1} × {n2} = {n1 * n2} = {toBase(n1 * n2, b)}{sub(b)}.
{n1 * n2} is the answer in base ten. Convert it to base {b}.

solution: Go through base ten: {placeSum(x, b)} and {placeSum(y, b)}.

questions.where: decMul(toBase(p4, b), str(q4)) != toBase(p4 * q4, b)
questions.prompt: Enow did four multiplications in base {b}. One is wrong. Which one?

right.truth: fromBase(toBase(p1 * q1, b), b) == fromBase(toBase(p1, b), b) * q1
fromBase(toBase(p2 * q2, b), b) == fromBase(toBase(p2, b), b) * q2
fromBase(toBase(p3 * q3, b), b) == fromBase(toBase(p3, b), b) * q3

wrong.truth: fromBase(decMul(toBase(p4, b), str(q4)), b) == fromBase(toBase(p4, b), b) * q4
wrong.explain: This product was worked out in base ten. In base {b} the answer is {toBase(p4 * q4, b)}{sub(b)}.
